title: Design Inventory Management System
summary: LLD inventory system: model stock as available vs reserved per SKU-warehouse bin, prevent oversell with per-bin locks, and expire reservations.

Design an Inventory Management System | Hello Interview

blocks.title: What the interviewer is really testing
blocks.text: This is **not a CRUD exercise**. The interviewer wants to see if you can model **contention over a scarce number**. Anyone can write `stock -= qty`. The test is: do you separate `onHand` from `available` from `reserved`, do you stop two threads from selling the last unit twice, and do you handle a reservation that never converts to a sale? If you jump to classes without nailing the reservation lifecycle, you fail.
The problem

Design an in-memory inventory management system for a retailer with multiple warehouses. It must track products, track how many units of each product sit in each warehouse, allow clients to check availability, reserve stock for an order, confirm or cancel that reservation, restock, and get alerted when stock runs low. The system must never oversell: the sum of confirmed plus unexpired reserved quantities can never exceed physical stock, even under concurrent reservations from many threads.

items: `addStock(sku, warehouseId, qty)` / `removeStock(sku, warehouseId, qty)` — inbound and damage / shrinkage.
`checkAvailability(sku, qty)` — is there enough sellable stock globally or per warehouse?
`reserve(sku, warehouseId, qty, orderId)` -> `reservationId` — soft-hold stock with a TTL.
`commitReservation(reservationId)` — convert hold into a sale, decrement physical.
`cancelReservation(reservationId)` / auto-expire — release hold back to available.

blocks.text: Clarify before you code

Strong candidates spend five minutes pinning the physics of stock before touching a class diagram. Inventory has at least three numbers that novices collapse into one, and every follow-up exploits that collapse. Force the interviewer to choose semantics now so your locks and state machine have something correct to enforce.

items.title: What does quantity mean?
items.text: Agree on three counters per bin: `onHand` is physical units present, `reserved` is soft-held for open orders, `available = onHand - reserved`. All sell decisions use `available`, never `onHand`. This one distinction drives the entire design.

items.title: Reserve then commit, or direct decrement?
items.text: Push for two-phase: `reserve` with expiry, then `commit` or `cancel`. Direct decrement cannot model abandoned carts and forces you to oversell or manually compensate. Ask what the reservation TTL should be and who sweeps expired holds.

items.title: Warehouse selection: caller picks or system allocates?
items.text: Does `reserve(sku, qty)` auto-split across warehouses nearest the customer, or must the caller pass `warehouseId`? Auto-allocation is a bin-packing and latency problem. For 45 minutes, make the caller pass `warehouseId` and expose a `findWarehousesWithStock(sku)` helper, then discuss allocation as a follow-up.

items.title: Can available go negative, and can two orders share the last unit?
items.text: Answer must be no. Ask if backorders are allowed. If yes, you need a separate backorder queue; if no, reservation must atomically check-and-hold. State your choice explicitly.

items.title: Scale and concurrency?
items.text: Single process or distributed? How many SKUs, warehouses, and reserves per second? This decides per-bin in-memory locks versus database optimistic versioning. Agree you will build single-process thread-safe and explain how it maps to a persistent version.

blocks.text: Approach 1 — the flat counter map

The naive answer is a `Map<String, Integer> stock` keyed by SKU with `if (stock.get(sku) >= qty) stock.put(sku, stock.get(sku) - qty)`. It looks clean, it passes a single-threaded demo, and it is wrong in every way that matters. It collapses physical and sellable into one integer, so you cannot distinguish sold from merely held. It has no warehouse dimension, so multi-node fulfillment is impossible. It has no reservation object, so abandoned carts leak stock forever. And the check-then-act is not atomic, so two threads both see `1 left` and both sell it.

Reject this explicitly in the interview. Name four failures: **lost update** under concurrency because read and write are not atomic, **stranded stock** because there is no expiry path, **no audit trail** because you mutated an integer instead of appending a reservation event, and **wrong granularity** because contention is per SKU-warehouse bin, not per global SKU. The fix is not adding `synchronized` to this method — that serializes all SKUs on one lock and still leaves the domain model broken. You need a different shape: a bin object with its own lock and a first-class reservation lifecycle. Trade-off stated plainly: the naive version is O(1) and trivial to write but sacrifices correctness; the real version costs more objects and locking logic to buy exactly-once sale semantics.

blocks.title: The oversell trap
blocks.text: Every failed solution does `if (available >= qty) available -= qty` without atomicity. Under two threads that interleaves to **-1**. The interviewer will run that interleaving mentally. Say upfront: **check-and-reserve must happen under the bin lock**, and `available` is derived, never stored independently.
Real design — bins, reservations, and per-bin locks

Model the warehouse bin as the aggregate root. A `Bin` holds `onHand` and `reserved` plus its own `ReentrantLock`. All mutations to that bin — restock, reserve, commit, cancel — happen under that single lock, so the check and the hold are one atomic step. Reservations are separate immutable-ish objects with `PENDING`, `COMMITTED`, `CANCELLED`, `EXPIRED` states and a deadline. `InventoryService` is a thin orchestrator: look up the bin, delegate to it, publish a low-stock event if the threshold is crossed. Observers handle alerts; a `ScheduledExecutorService` sweeps expired holds. Why this shape? Per-bin locking gives you parallelism across SKUs for free — Coke and Pepsi never block each other — while serializing only true competitors for the same physical shelf. The cost is more locks to manage and a background sweeper to reason about, but that is the price of never overselling without a global bottleneck. Alternative of one global lock is simpler to prove correct but caps throughput at one reservation at a time; alternative of lock-free atomics per integer reintroduces split-brain between `onHand` and `reserved`.

blocks.title: Domain structure
blocks.caption: Bin is the contention boundary.

blocks.text: Read the class diagram as contention boundaries, not just nouns. `Product` and `Warehouse` are dumb identity records — no behavior, no locks — because they are never contended. `Bin` owns the invariant `reserved <= onHand` and is the only class allowed to mutate counts, which is why it owns the lock. `Reservation` is a value plus state machine; it never mutates a bin directly, the service does that under the bin lock to keep ordering deterministic. `StockListener` is an Observer so alerting never blocks the reserve path — slow email or webhook code cannot hold a bin lock. Trade-off: this indirection adds a map lookup per operation, but it isolates failure domains and keeps the hot path to two hash lookups plus one uncontended lock acquisition in the common case.

blocks.text: Concurrency — the make-or-break follow-up

The interviewer will ask some variant of: ten buyers race for the last two units, how do you guarantee you sell exactly two? Answer with three sentences and then point at the code. One: contention scope is the bin, so `reserve` acquires that bin's `ReentrantLock` before reading `available`. Two: check and mutation happen inside the same critical section, so the interleaving that causes oversell is structurally impossible — there is no unlock between test and hold. Three: `commit` and `cancel` re-check `PENDING` status inside the same lock, so double-commit or commit-after-expiry cannot double-decrement. Then name the trade-offs like a senior. Per-bin pessimistic locking is easy to reason about and gives high parallelism across bins, but a hot SKU in one warehouse still serializes — that is correct serialization, not a bottleneck you can remove without risking oversell. The alternative, optimistic versioning with a `version` column in a database, allows higher throughput under low contention but forces retries under high contention and pushes complexity to the caller. For distributed deployments, say you would replace the in-memory lock with a row-level `SELECT FOR UPDATE` or a conditional update `WHERE available >= qty` plus a unique reservation id for idempotency, and run the expiry sweeper as a single leader or with claim-and-sweep to avoid double-expiry.

blocks.title: Say this line verbatim
blocks.text: **Never store `available` as a field.** Store `onHand` and `reserved`, derive `available`. Two stored counters that must stay consistent will diverge; one derived value cannot. That single sentence signals you have built this before.
Follow-ups to have ready

items.title: Allocate across warehouses?
items.text: Greedy nearest-with-stock first, or split proportionally. This becomes a short transaction across multiple bin locks — lock bins in sorted key order to avoid deadlock, reserve all-or-nothing, and roll back partial holds on failure. Trade-off: multi-bin atomicity costs coordinated locking versus single-bin simplicity.

items.title: Idempotent reserve/commit?
items.text: Attach `orderId` as idempotency key: if the same order retries, return the existing reservation instead of creating a duplicate. Store order-to-reservation mapping. Costs memory, buys exactly-once semantics over flaky networks.

items.title: Persistence?
items.text: Map bins to a table with `(sku, warehouse_id, on_hand, reserved, version)`. Use optimistic locking on version or atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE on_hand - reserved >= qty`. Keep the sweeper in the database with an index on `expires_at`. Trade-off: throughput drops versus memory, durability wins.

items.title: Low-stock and replenishment?
items.text: Observer fires when `available <= threshold`; a reorder policy (Strategy pattern) computes purchase quantity. Do not reorder inside the bin lock — publish an event and let a consumer act. Keeps hot path fast at the cost of eventual replenishment.

items.title: Race on expiry vs commit?
items.text: Both paths re-check status and deadline under the same bin lock; only the first wins, the second sees non-PENDING and returns false. Requires the deadline check inside the lock, not before it.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state unprompted

items: Reserve zero or negative quantity, unknown SKU, unknown warehouse — reject, never create a reservation.
Reserve more than available by exactly one — the boundary the interviewer will test.
Double `commit` on the same id, `cancel` after `commit`, `commit` after expiry — all return `false` with no count change.
Expiry fires in the same millisecond as `commit` — lock ordering decides one winner; state it.
Restock arrives while holds are pending — `onHand` rises, `available` rises, pending holds unaffected.
Remove more than `available` via damage / shrinkage — clamp and require manager override; never let `onHand` go below `reserved`.
Hot SKU thundering herd — per-bin lock serializes correctly; mention queueing or backpressure rather than weakening the invariant.
Clock skew for TTL in distributed version — use monotonic lease or database timestamp, not client time.

blocks.title: 45-minute plan
blocks.text: Minutes 0-5: clarify the three counters and reserve-then-commit. Minutes 5-10: draw bins, reservations, and the state machine. Minutes 10-25: code `Bin` plus `reserve` and `commit` with per-bin locks. Minutes 25-35: handle expiry, cancel, and low-stock observer. Minutes 35-45: drive concurrency, idempotency, multi-warehouse allocation, and persistence mapping. Close by restating the invariant: **reserved never exceeds onHand, and every hold has exactly one terminal state.**
